articles.summary: Artificial intelligence company Anthropic made a strong stock market debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, with its shares closing 17.07% higher at $97.17
articles.body: Artificial intelligence company Anthropic made a strong stock market debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, with its shares closing 17.07% higher at $97.17 after opening more than 30% above their initial public offering (IPO) price.The maker of AI chatbot Claude raised $81.31 billion through its initial public offering (IPO), setting a new record for the largest IPO at initial pricing and surpassing SpaceX's initial $75 billion offering.The blockbuster listing has drawn attention to the growing investor appetite for AI companies and opened up a new opportunity for investors worldwide to participate in the sector's growth.For Indian investors who missed the IPO, buying shares at the original offer price is no longer an option.They can, however, explore investing in Anthropic through the US stock market, where shares will be available at the prevailing market price. This could be higher or lower than the IPO price, depending on demand and market movements.Their opportunity to invest will come through the US stock market, where Anthropic is listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT.Once trading begins, investors will be able to buy shares at the prevailing market price, which could be higher than the IPO price.The offering comprises 980 million Class A common shares. Anthropic is selling 956.35 million shares, while existing shareholders are offering the remaining 23.65 million.The company will not receive proceeds from the sale of shares by existing shareholders.The IPO is expected to give Anthropic a valuation of more than $1 trillion, placing it among the world's most valuable technology companies.How can Indian investors buy Anthropic shares?Indian residents can purchase US-listed stocks through overseas brokerage accounts that provide access to Nasdaq-listed companies. These investments can be made under the Reserve Bank of India's Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS).Investors first need to open an account with a platform offering access to US stocks and complete the required KYC formalities. They can then remit funds from an Indian bank account through an authorised banking channel and use the money to buy shares once they are available for trading.GIFT City-based investment platforms may also offer another route to overseas equities, depending on their products and regulatory arrangements. Investors should check whether their chosen platform supports trading in Anthropic shares before opening an account or transferring funds.Platforms such as Zerodha, Groww and HDFC Securities offer access to overseas stocks.How much can Indians invest in US stocks?Under the RBI's LRS framework, resident individuals can remit up to $250,000 per financial year for permitted overseas transactions.This includes investments in foreign stocks and overseas-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), as well as eligible expenses such as travel and education.The annual limit can be used entirely for investments in US stocks if the investor does not need to set aside any portion for other permitted overseas expenses during that financial year.For example, an investor who has no other planned overseas expenses, such as education payments or travel, can use the full $250,000 remittance allowance to invest in foreign equities, subject to applicable rules.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
articles.summary: Anthropic’s IPO went better than expected. Demand was hot, Wall Street jumped at its first chance to buy in to a frontier AI model. The stock got a nice bounce.
articles.body: Anthropic’s IPO went better than expected. Demand was hot, Wall Street jumped at its first chance to buy in to a frontier AI model. The stock got a nice bounce. What a relief for the beaten-down AI industry? Not exactly. The rest of the tech stock market wasn’t invited to Anthropic’s party on Thursday. The Nasdaq slumped. Again. Friday looks like more of the same: The Nasdaq fell 5.28% and is now down for the year. Even Anthropic’s stock was down 8.5% Friday — a consequence of getting swept up in the AI malaise that’s been brewing for six straight weeks … and the fact that its underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley aren’t working quite as hard to prop up the stock like they did on Thursday. Buying shares of Anthropic is a wager on the future of AI, a bet that the AI-fueled economy will someday soon transition from investment in construction sites to profit generated from customers paying for large language models to revolutionize research, medicine, manufacturing and the way the world works. That bet may pay off big time. But in the here and now, Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO didn’t change the narrative that has been worrying Wall Street since early October: Regulation could be around the corner, AI investment may slow down, valuations are sky high, and some of the early bets placed on the transformative technology may fail to pay off. What’s got Wall Street worried AI has been on wobbly footing since October 6, when the market last hit a record. Since then, the AI-spending-will-just-keep-growing-forever narrative has absorbed blow after blow. CoreWeave. It started when CoreWeave’s bond yields rose to 15% (when the company’s return on investment was only 9%). That sent alarm bells ringing that maybe some parts of the AI industry were valued way too high — particularly neoclouds like CoreWeave that buy computing power at high prices and lease it out to other companies. It’s not a universally bad business, but hasn’t exactly proven to be a sustainable one. In the early stages of every tech boom, every company is a winner. During the crypto boom, the Long Island Iced Tea Company put “blockchain” in its name and its stock exploded. But, eventually, losers start to emerge. CoreWeave may not end up in that category, but its bond price collapse warned investors that some AI bets may fail. The blue tsunami. Another shock to the AI system: Democrats’ sweeping victory in the November 3 midterm elections, including the surprise win for Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa – who called for an extended AI data center moratorium and stricter guardrails around AI. Texas is home to 25% of the country’s planned computing capacity buildout, and Democratic governors who champion AI regulation will oversee 45% of that planned capacity starting in January, according to Goldman Sachs. That dealt another big blow to AI stocks in the wake of the midterms. Nvidia. And then there was Jensen Huang’s scandal. The former Nvidia CEO and president was the driving force behind the circular financing deals that have powered AI’s growth over the past several years. Nvidia acts as a kind of central bank for AI companies, doling out chips in exchange for equity stakes, buying in to massive data center projects and guaranteeing leases that many AI businesses would otherwise be unable to afford. Huang’s resignation ignited fears on Wall Street that a more conservative leader would replace him — concerns that appeared validated when interim CEO Colette Kress (a skeptic of some of Huang’s riskier deals) announced last week that Nvidia was getting out of the selling-chips-to-China business. The Nvidia scandal forced the Commerce Department’s hand after taking a mostly lenient approach in the company’s business of selling chips to Southeast Asian companies – even when evidence suggested some of those companies were shipping those chips to China to circumvent export restrictions. Commerce put in place a new rule last week that required sign-off in deals to companies in certain countries, including Singapore — home of Megaspeed, where an executive was wrapped up in Huang’s scandal. Now swept up in this mess: AMD, an Nvidia competitor that was supposed to be a winner from Nvidia’s scandals. Instead, a short seller issued a report Thursday claiming that AMD’s chips are being sold on China’s black market. AMD’s stock tumbled nearly 8% Thursday and another 13% Friday, as investors worried it could be the subject of the next investigation. Reality check Despite the recent blows, AI hasn’t been knocked down by any means. And this isn’t exactly new: As valuations have gone through the roof in recent years, Big Tech has gone through bouts of Wall Street worry before. You don’t need to look that far back. Between June and August, the Nasdaq fell 9.7% over fears that AI infrastructure required too much spending (measured in the literal trillions of dollars) and wouldn’t return profits anytime soon. And in 2022, the entire tech sector was effectively in recession, briefly dragging the broader market into bear market territory (a 20% decline). Now, the Nasdaq is in correction — a decline of more than 10% from a recent peak. It has tumbled 18% over the past six weeks and may be headed further south — but corrections are normal and healthy market functions. The broader S&P 500 also closed in correction, falling for a seventh-straight day. “We’re climbing a wall of worry,” said Cathie Wood, CEO of tech fund Ark Invest, in an interview on CNBC Friday morning. If you are wondering why the market is worried about AI, Anthropic spelled it out for you. It spent more than 90 pages of its IPO prospectus detailing its many, many risk factors. Among them: Both concern that its customers are slowing their spending on frontier AI and worry that it may not be able to buy enough computing power to satisfy demand. It could lose both ways. And, of course, Anthropic warned that its technology could wipe out humanity. None of this means AI is a bust. There are many signs it isn’t: Nvidia gave a strong earnings report and raised its outlook last week. And don’t forget: Anthropic had a very strong debut despite Friday’s decline. Even if Anthropic continues to sink, that doesn’t mean its IPO was a bust. Facebook tumbled 20% in the days following its debut on the public market and lost more than 50% of its value within months. It took the company around 14 months to return to its IPO price. Since then: its stock has gained 1,469%. The challenges for AI are real and undeniable. But the potential promise of the revolutionary technology hasn’t changed just because of a recent string of setbacks. “The revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding,” said James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics. “This doesn’t mean we think the technology is a dud, nor that demand will collapse.”

articles.title: Markets plunge: Nasdaq erases 2026 gains, S&P and Dow enter corrections
articles.summary: A bruising stock market sell-off continued despite a record-setting IPO by Anthropic, dashing hopes it would revive sentiment on the AI trade.
articles.body: The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks. The dramatic sell off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth writ large higher for the first half of the year. Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting ishares just a few dollars above its IPO price. Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant. With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid-19 pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year. The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%. The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process. While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weeks-long slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices, rising interest rates, mounting corporate debt loads, stubborn inflation, supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices. The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China. “The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.” Alongside the stock sell off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China. “The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday. For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove nettlesome. Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation. “They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.” A prolonged downturn could begin to cut more deeply into economic growth, he said. “If you have enough of a protracted downturn, which we really haven’t had since 2007-2009 in terms of length and duration, that’s when you’d really start to worry,” he said.

articles.title: Flipkart sale shift hits Walmart’s Q3 growth, Q4 boost expected
articles.summary: Flipkart’s Big Billion Days sale shift cut Walmart International Q3 growth by 5 points; Walmart expects a Q4 boost as festive sales revenue is recognized.
articles.body: BENGALURU: The change in timing of Flipkart’s Big Billion Days festive sale reduced Walmart International’s sales growth by five percentage points in the third quarter of FY27. The US retail giant expects a corresponding boost in the fourth quarter as the sale’s revenue gets reflected in its results.The shift also pulled down Walmart’s overall sales growth by one percentage point in the quarter. Walmart owns a majority stake in Flipkart, India’s largest e-commerce marketplace, and also operates fashion platform Myntra.“We faced a 100 basis point headwind to top-line growth in Q3,” Walmart chief financial officer John David Rainey said during the company’s earnings call on Thursday. He attributed the impact to the timing of Flipkart’s flagship sale, which will be reflected in its fourth-quarter results this year.Flipkart held its 11-day Big Billion Days sale from Oct 9 this year. The event was held in September last year. The change pushed the sale into a different reporting quarter for Walmart, which follows a February-January financial year.Walmart International reported a 7% increase in net sales to $35.9 billion in the third quarter, compared with $33.5 billion a year earlier. Excluding currency fluctuations, sales grew 3.3%.The timing change also affected Walmart International’s e-commerce and advertising businesses. E-commerce sales fell 2% during the quarter, while advertising revenue declined 15%. Walmart attributed both declines to the absence of Big Billion Days sales from the quarter’s reported numbers.The company expects the festive sale to add around one percentage point to its overall sales growth in the fourth quarter. Its international business is also expected to see a corresponding benefit.The Big Billion Days event reportedly recorded 20%-22% year-on-year growth in orders, units sold and buyers during the 11-day period.At the group level, Walmart reported a 5.2% increase in third-quarter revenue to $188.8 billion. Global e-commerce sales grew 17%, despite the impact of the Flipkart sale timing.Walmart also raised its FY27 net sales growth forecast to 4.9%-5.2% in constant currency, from 4%-5% earlier. articles.title: Michael Burry says he 'tried to warn' investors that Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius were headed for trouble
articles.summary: Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame said he tried to warn investors a selloff was coming, and he sees deeper issues than Jensen Huang and politics.
articles.body:
Michael Burry says he told buyers of AI infrastructure stocks they were headed for trouble.

Burry posted on X following the slump in CoreWeave, Nebius, Nvidia, and microchip stocks in general.

The "Big Short" investor said it reflects deeper issues than the Jensen Huang scandal and politics.

Michael Burry has a message for everyone who bet on AI infrastructure stocks and lost money: I told you so.

"CoreWeave, Nebius, Nvidia, semis, I tried to warn you all ," Burry said in an X post on Thursday. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

Nvidia shares opened about 4% lower on Friday, while CoreWeave and Nebius fell around 7%.

The trio are down about 42%, 55%, and 65% respectively from their intraday highs on October 6, the day before the current AI drawdown began. The NYSE Semiconductor Index has slumped by about 30% over the same period.

On November 11, the day before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO, Burry urged shareholders in a Substack post to " get out " of the AI chipmaker's stock. He predicted it would grow more slowly and its profit margins would shrink without the prolific dealmaker in charge.

Burry cautioned that Nvidia partners such as Nebius and CoreWeave — so-called "neoclouds" that build data centers and rent access to Nvidia chips and other AI infrastructure — could be caught in the fallout in a November 12 post.

He said they've "benefited greatly from Nvidia's market power and largesse, which seems to have entered a new paradigm now."

Burry declared on August 12 that "Nebius is what the top of a boom looks like." The stock closed at $259 that day, 62% higher than its November 19 close.

A week earlier, on August 6, Burry said he couldn't resist shorting Nebius and Oracle, saying it was a "bit like shooting fish in a barrel." He's also shorted Nvidia, CoreWeave, and chip indexes this year.

Burry has been loudly skeptical of the stratospheric rise in AI stocks since he pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing a Substack about his personal investments a year ago.

The contrarian investor, one of the few people to predict and profit from the collapse of the mid-2000s housing bubble, has warned AI companies are overinvesting in fast-depreciating assets such as microchips and data centers.

He's also called out their aggressive accounting, circular-financing deals, and dangerous levels of debt and off-balance-sheet liabilities.

Burry emphasized in a late Thursday post on X that he has far deeper concerns about Nvidia and its partners and peers than Huang's alleged extramarital affairs, and a potentially less AI-friendly environment with Democrats in charge of the House and Senate.

"If you think this is still all about an affair and some politics, you're not thinking hard enough," he wrote.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Taj at 124: Opens 400th property; aims to have over 700 by 2030
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Just ahead of completing 124 years, Taj parent Indian Hotel Co Ltd (IHCL) opened its 400th operating hotel on Friday with the Taj Yelahanka,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Just ahead of completing 124 years, Taj parent Indian Hotel Co Ltd (IHCL) opened its 400th operating hotel on Friday with the Taj Yelahanka, Bengaluru, becoming that landmark property. Tata Group founder Jamsetji Tata had on Dec 1, 1903, opened the first hotel — Taj Mahal Palace — in what was then Bombay. IHCL has become the first Indian hospitality company to reach the 400-mark. It currently has a portfolio of 690 hotels including 290 in the pipeline globally across four continents, 15 countries and over 300 locations.IHCL MD and CEO Puneet Chhatwal said: “Taj Yelahanka, Bengaluru… marks the milestone of IHCL’s 400th operating hotel.… We will continue to pursue opportunities… leveraging our complementary strengths in asset development and hotel operations through a capital-light management model.”Under its “Accelerate 2030” plan, IHCL plans to have over 700 properties by 2030. “IHCL will expand its brandscape with the launch of new brands, tapping the heterogeneous market landscape and taking its portfolio to 700 plus hotels by 2030. Doubling its consolidated revenue to Rs 15,000 crore, scaling new and reimagined businesses to a 25%+ share of revenue and continuing to generate industry-leading margins and return on investment, while maintaining its renowned service excellence,” says the plan. The group expects management fee to cross Rs 1,000 crores by 2030. “The portfolio expansion strategy focuses on strengthening IHCL’s domestic dominance in the Indian subcontinent while enhancing its international prominence by expanding into key international markets. By efficiently deploying capital and pursuing strategic acquisitions, the Company optimised its portfolio mix, achieving a 63:37 split between capital-light and capital-heavy inventory to enhance flexibility and resilience,” says the plan.Under “Accelerate 2030,” the group’s focus will be on driving top-line growth with 75% revenue contribution from traditional businesses and management fees and 25%+ from new and reimagined businesses by 2030.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: The economy is doing better than you think — just not for everyone
articles.summary: When you hear that the U.S. economy is good, bad, strong or weak, always remember that it depends on where the data is coming from — and who you’re asking.
articles.body:
2026 is almost over, and as we head into the new year, with a new Congress , many are wondering what’s ahead for the U.S. economy.

Barring any catastrophic events — an AI or crypto bust, a terror attack, more war in the Middle East or elsewhere — so far, so good. In fact, the U.S. economy, and the small businesses that employ half of our workers and make up almost half of our GDP , seem to be doing just fine.

On the downside, producer prices are up , with increases running more than 6 percent over the past year. That doesn’t bode well for inflation in the months ahead. Higher sustained inflation means not only higher costs, but potentially higher Treasury yields and higher-than-average mortgage rates, which have contributed to the big fall in existing home sales. People in the real estate sector are hurting.

Speaking of interest, the U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates again before the end of the year, which will make the cost of borrowing higher (the prime rate for business loans is now at 7 percent). The New York Federal Reserve reports that household debt is historically high, and approximately 5 percent of outstanding household debt was delinquent, up from 4.7 percent in the preceding quarter. Approximately 135,000 consumers had new bankruptcy notations added to their credit reports, according to the same report.

However, inflation excluding gas has cooled a bit, oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and prices at the pump have fallen below $4 on average for the first time since July. Credit card debt also reached record levels, but the rate at which balances transition into serious delinquency improved slightly. This gives consumers more ability to spend.

And what about those consumers? They drive everything, and they’re not slowing down.

Retail sales continue to increase . Target says more shoppers are visiting their stores ahead of the holiday season. The National Retail Association is predicting a 4.2 percent growth in holiday sales over last year. Visa is expecting a record increase in holiday spending at retailers. Adobe is saying that consumers will spend 6.7 percent more online than the previous holiday season. That’s great news for merchants.

There’s also good news for small businesses. American Express, which started Small Business Saturday, says that the annual shopping day after Black Friday will be another success, with 88 percent of consumers they surveyed saying they are likely to shop at small businesses this holiday season — the highest percentage since 2012.

Small businesses, overall, appear to be weathering the challenges of higher costs, tariffs and a tight job market. Many are uncertain about what’s ahead but, according to one survey from payroll and HR provider Gusto, 86 percent of small-business owners say their companies are meeting or exceeding their original expectations and that they are confident in their own abilities to grow and profit. The National Federation of Business’s closely watched Small Business Optimism Index declined slightly last month, just below its historical average, but its Uncertainty Index fell even more.

The Institute for Supply Management reports that economic activity in the manufacturing sector expanded in October for the 10th consecutive month. The services sector also continued its record expansion in October, which, according to the ISM, marks the 28th consecutive month in expansion territory. Orders for durable goods also jumped higher than anticipated.

The job picture still looks pretty good, too. HR firm Paychex says that small employers are showing “resilience” and continuing to add jobs (although hourly rates are still lagging inflation). ADP reports that private-sector employees added 86,000 new jobs just in October, and that overall gross pay increased 4.7 percent year over year. Unemployment claims remain at historically low levels.

It means that the U.S. economy is doing well. But that doesn’t mean it’s doing well for everyone. That’s because it never does well for everyone. There are hundreds of millions of people in this country and more than 30 million small businesses . How they’re faring depends on things like we’re they’re located, what industry they’re in, how the weather is and whether or not their business or livelihood is exposed to factors — tariffs, oil prices, etc. — that are out of their control.

When you hear that the U.S. economy is good, bad, strong or weak, always remember that it depends on where the data is coming from and who you’re asking. So how’s the economy? Seems pretty good to me. But then again, that depends.

Gene Marks is founder of the Marks Group, a small-business consulting firm.

articles.summary: Expone que todos los días recibe quejas de otros trabajadores nacionales del sector
articles.body: España tiene serios problemas para vender sus aguacates. La clave no está en la producción, pues nuestra nación está consagrada como uno de los países con más cosechas de este producto. Sin embargo, cada día ven como las estanterías de los supermercados se llenan de artículos importados. A priori, la primera explicación que se puede venir a la mente es la diferencia de precio. Pero no. Mientras que muchos aguacates extranjeros se venden por más de cinco euros el kilo, los aguacates españoles están a tres euros. Es por eso que desde Europa Agricultura Product muestran su desconcierto con lo que está ocurriendo. El agricultor Pascual Cabeda asegura que no encuentra ninguna “explicación” para este asunto. Además, tiene un mensaje para los consumidores españoles: “Por favor, cuando vayáis a comprar un aguacate, mirar el origen y buscar el aguacate español”. Y es que hace apenas unas semanas que comenzó la campaña del aguacate nacional, que puede durar hasta el próximo mes de mayo. Por otro lado, desde EAP siguen insistiendo en trabajar para dar salida a las cosechas de los trabajadores. Por otro lado, recomiendan a los consumidores pagar un precio justo, algo que se puede obtener con el aguacate español. De él destacan que es de máxima calidad y frescura. Además, comprándolos, estarías ayudando a los agricultores nacionales. El origen del problema, según analizan algunos expertos, es que España consume más aguacates de los que puede producir, y además la producción española es muy estacional y está concentrada en determinadas zonas. Es decir, como país no tenemos la capacidad para abastecer la demanda del mercado durante todo el año. Por eso, se importa del extranjero. Se calcula que la producción española está en torno a las 120.000 toneladas, mientras que la importación extranjera es de 260.000.

articles.title: Apple's secret AI agent shows John Ternus is done sitting out the AI race
articles.summary: Apple's AI agent plans hit Meta and Anthropic stock before the job listing revealing its ambitions disappeared.
articles.body:
Apple ( AAPL ) scrubbed a job listing by Friday that showed it building its own AI agent. By then, Meta ( META ) and Anthropic ( ANT ) stock had already slid on what the post revealed.

The listing described "an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does," browsing the web, working across apps, and writing code, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported Thursday .

Then it vanished. "Apple killed the job listing, which is typical when they reveal too much about future plans," Gurman posted on X .

It's the clearest sign yet that Apple is done watching the AI boom from the bleachers. John Ternus, who replaced Tim Cook as CEO on Sept. 1, has been pressing software chief Craig Federighi to move faster , Bloomberg reported this month. Apple is aiming for a launch as soon as late next year.

Investors didn't wait. Anthropic stock fell nearly 5% in late trading Thursday after the report, below the low of its first session as a public company . Meta stock fell about 1%, while Apple shares rose Thursday evening. On Friday, Apple was holding up far better than Meta and the Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) as tech sold off.

The worry sits on Apple's own App Store shelf. AI assistants from its rivals hold four of the marketplace's top six free apps, led by Meta's Muse agent at No. 2. "Over 10 million people activating in the span of 45 days. I mean, that's pretty incredible," AMD ( AMD ) CEO Lisa Su told Yahoo Finance about Muse.

Apple has been easing in all year, picking Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Gemini to power the new Siri in January. "As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users," Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.

Apple also controls the door. Its next Mac update will require users to click through 14 steps to let ChatGPT run their computer, up from four today, Bloomberg reported.

Somebody still has to pay for the AI build-out. So far, it isn't Apple.

Apple's capital spending , or capex — what a company spends on long-lasting assets like buildings and equipment — fell nearly 30% to about $9 billion in its latest fiscal year. Meanwhile, Microsoft ( MSFT ), Meta, Alphabet, and Amazon ( AMZN ) spent more than $600 billion over four quarters.

Apple's research budget jumped about $11 billion, more than its entire capex bill. For the heavy lifting, it rents, paying Google about $1 billion a year for Gemini, according to Bloomberg.

An agent could change that math. Agents grind through multistep tasks in the background, which takes far more computing than answering a question. CFO Kevan Parekh said Apple is "in very, very early stages of understanding the kind of mix of those costs."

articles.title: Nasdaq wipes out gains for the year as Anthropic IPO fails to quell AI nerves
articles.summary: A punishing sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade.
articles.body: A punishing sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and posted its seventh consecutive day of losses — its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street started bracing for what became the Covid pandemic. The Nasdaq faced even steeper losses on Friday, dropping 5.28%. It is now down more than 2% for the year. The tech-focused Nasdaq hit a record high on October 6, and was up as much as 18.7% on the year. Since that all-time high, the index has slumped, erasing all those gains. “It’s a meltdown right now,” Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN in an email. “So much bearish sentiment around tech and AI.” Even Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine Friday, with shares in the AI lab dropping 8.5%. They closed at $88.91, just above the company’s IPO of $83. The Dow fell 950 points, or 1.93%, posting its fifth consecutive day of losses of more than 1%. The Dow dropped 8% this week, its worst week since March 2020. The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction on Friday, trading down more than 10% from their respective peaks on August 5 and October 6. They join the Nasdaq, which closed in correction earlier this month and is now down 18% since its record high on October 6. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 suffered their worst week since early April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s tariff plans rocked global markets. Stocks associated with the AI trade have been in a serious rough patch for weeks now. But with Anthropic’s buzzy IPO now in the rear-view mirror, traders’ concerns about the broader industry are once again coming to the fore. “There is a real exodus out of tech stocks,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at the online brokerage platform Interactive Brokers, told CNN. “Buy the dip has been taking a back seat to sell the rally – or just sell.” “The tech sector is just getting walloped,” Sosnick said. Investors are grappling with a bevy of concerns, from uncertainty over how newly elected Democratic governors will impact the pace of the data center buildout to uncertainty about the future of Nvidia’s role in powering the AI industry’s growth after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. “There is a fear that maybe there is too much froth and enthusiasm in the tech bet given all the risks out there,” said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management. Kelly noted that corrections are “inevitable” and there is “nothing particularly ominous” about a correction given how much US stocks have rallied in recent years. “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu. At the moment, it looks like a mild cold, and it should be over in a week or two,” he said. Another growing concern for investors: Companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the AI buildout, using their own cash and also tapping the debt and equity markets to raise more capital. For awhile, investors cheered the AI spending. But now, they’re getting more serious about demanding evidence of return on investment. “The market was already questioning some of the cost-benefit analysis … and you’re coming off of relatively euphoric levels. Put all that together, that’s a lot for the market to bear,” Sosnick at Interactive Brokers told CNN. In a sign of growing nervousness among investors, the VIX, which tracks expectations for volatility and is known as Wall Street’s ‘fear gauge,’ surged 86% this week and closed at 35.89 on Friday — its highest level in 19 months. Generally, a level above 20 indicates heightened investor uncertainty. The sell-off sent investors looking for safer corners of the market, like US Treasury bonds, which rallied sharply on Friday. Classic defensive sectors of the stock market, like consumer staples and healthcare, also advanced. Corners of the AI trade that have been in the spotlight in recent weeks were among the names under pressure. CoreWeave, the neocloud backed by Nvidia, slumped 12% Friday. CoreWeave’s IPO price in March 2025 was $40 a share — it’s trading at $39.51 now, wiping out all gains since since it debuted on the market. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday, its worst day in almost two years. The chip giant tumbled 22.9% on the week, posting its worst week since October 2008. Nvidia has plunged 47.5% since its October 6 peak, shedding $2.7 trillion in market value. That’s larger than the individual market value of every company in the S&P 500 except Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia itself. The sell-off has been so severe that tech stocks may suddenly look cheap to some investors. US tech stock valuations, as measured by the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500’s info tech sector, entered Friday at their lowest level since March 2020, according to FactSet. As for Nvidia? The forward P/E ratio for the next 12 months is the lowest since 2002. That has some strategists suggesting that widespread fears might be overblown. “I don’t fully understand it, as the fundamentals don’t really justify all this selling,” said Sundaram from CFRA Research. “But right now, it’s sell now and worry about the fundamentals later.”

articles.title: US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing.
articles.body:
Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.

On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT).

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.

“Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.

Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively.

Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent.

More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.

Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.

articles.title: Microsoft to Pay Top Cloud Workers More, Crack Down on Others
articles.summary: Microsoft Corp. is making pay more performance-based in its crucial cloud division, the latest tech industry attempt to push employees to work even harder.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. is making pay more performance-based in its crucial cloud division, the latest tech industry attempt to push employees to work even harder.

Those employees who receive top marks will get additional stock awards while workers with lower results will have formal meetings with their managers, according to a memo sent by Arun Ulagaratchagan, executive vice president at the Azure cloud computing division.

"Pay-for-performance only works if we are equally rigorous on both sides: recognizing exceptional impact and being honest when performance falls short," Ulagaratchagan wrote in the memo, which was reviewed by Bloomberg News.

Many big tech companies are pushing employees to do more, including by more regularly axing those they deem low performers. Microsoft has shed tens of thousands of workers in waves of layoffs in recent years, and is currently offering buyouts to about 60,000 of its employees.

"A world-class team like Azure requires world-class talent," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "Yesterday, we shared an update to our compensation model in Azure, which includes meaningful additional awards for our strongest performing colleagues. We also shared an update on how we will ensure employees have clear expectations and receive timely, direct feedback from their managers."

Elon Musk in 2022 famously gave Twitter employees the choice to be "extremely hardcore," or take a severance payment. Earlier this year, Business Insider reported that an executive at Alphabet Inc.'s Google told employees in his organization that those who weren't "all in" on AI could have a voluntary buyout package.

"Meeting today's bar means closing previous performance gaps and demonstrating a meaningful step-change in impact," Ulagaratchagan wrote. "AI is reshaping how the world works, and competition has never been more intense."

articles.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on companies that build AI data centers overseas
articles.summary: President Trump plans to restrict U.S. companies from building data centers overseas — another example of his embrace of AI infrastructure most people oppose.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Friday that he plans to restrict U.S. companies from building data centers overseas — the latest instance of the president embracing the construction of massive tech facilities that a majority of Americans oppose. Back in Washington after a trip to Asia, Trump said the restrictions were necessary to prevent AI infrastructure from leaving U.S. shores. “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump told reporters in the White House briefing room. “We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country,” he said. He added that the U.S. would tax any company that attempted to build a data center abroad. “We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” he said. The comments signaled a potential new headache for the artificial intelligence industry, on a day when stock markets tumbled and not even the record-setting IPO this week of Anthropic could soothe investors’ fears about the sustainability of AI stocks. They were also the latest example of Trump’s forceful advocacy for AI data centers, a position that puts him squarely at odds with the majority of Americans. “You ought to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said Friday. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don’t shut them off.” Trump has previously attacked state and local efforts to roll back data center construction, saying in August that they should only be stopped if communities “want to end up being backwards and poor.” “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” Trump wrote in a social media post. During this year’s midterm elections, data centers proved a key sticking point for voters, who overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised to curb their proliferation. On Wall Street, the massive wins by Democrats who pledged to rein in data centers put a fresh dent in an already-ailing AI stock trade, as investors digested the prospect that tech companies’ computing resources would be further crimped. Since Nov. 4, the S&P 500 has declined approximately 9%, though a confluence of other factors has also contributed to the brutal sell-off. It is not clear how Trump’s foreign data center ban would be implemented; a White House representative did not immediately reply to a request for comment Friday. Trump admitted that he had not yet told his staff about the plan. “I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump mused. “I’m telling them now — they’re here, many of them are here — and we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can’t. But we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it.”

articles.title: 7 reasons why tech stocks are getting hammered again
articles.summary: The tech sell-off has returned. And it's ugly.
articles.body:
So much for the much-hyped Anthropic ( ANT ) IPO on Thursday lifting the spirits of tech investors ahead of the holidays.

Lost in all the Anthropic IPO coverage yesterday was the fact that, while the stock finished up nicely on its debut day, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 2.2%.

The selling pressure in wider tech intensified on Friday, underpinned by several key reasons, pros say.

"This sell-off has been driven by a perfect storm," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives wrote.

He listed the catalysts for the latest tech rout: "1) The Blue Tidal Wave win and fears about an anti-AI/anti-datacenter DC, 2) losing the global leader of the AI Revolution Jensen in his black eye moment, 3) China driven regulatory concerns across the rest of semis/memory stocks (e.g. AMD short report yesterday), 4) multiple market clearing events which have just led to more selling, 5) Anthropic IPO being a massive success but marginally reducing liquidity from other tech names, 6) significant fund P&L pain diminishing buying power, and 7) sticky inflation and hawkish Fed speak with concerns around more hikes and constricting financial conditions."

Anthropic is getting roped into the sell-off in day two of public company life. Shares of the model builder dropped 12% in afternoon trading on Friday as investors booked profits after a frenetic first day of trading.

Anthropic made a monster debut on Wall Street Thursday, with shares opening at $111.50 a little before noon ET, a 34% premium to the $83 IPO price.

But the AI company's stock couldn't hold on to its early gains: The stock closed at $97.17, up 17% on the day.

That closing price gave Anthropic a market capitalization of about $1.28 trillion, or roughly $1.75 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

Wall Street is still out there defending tech stocks, especially at valuations not seen in years.

D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said a "clean" earnings report from Nvidia ( NVDA ) this week and a successful Anthropic IPO "clear the way for AI-driven stocks to start coming back."

Ives added, "We continue to believe a diversified AI approach to the market is the way to own the winners and derivatives of the AI Revolution into 2027: This is a painful tech sell-off that is heavily discounting this 4th Industrial Revolution thesis will take place over the next few years … and that is the wrong move in our view."

articles.title: Chips suffer worst week since 2001 as the Nasdaq nears a bear market
articles.summary: Chip stocks are falling at a 2001 pace, but most of the market is holding up.
articles.body:
Wall Street is wrapping up a kind of week it has seen only five other times since World War II. Two of them came in 2008 and 2001.

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell every day this week, with four drops of 1% or more. That had happened only in 1962, 1974, 1978, the week after the 9/11 attacks in 2001 and October 2008, according to Bespoke Investment Group .

Friday brought the sharpest leg down. The S&P 500 fell nearly 4% and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) more than 5%, wiping out the Nasdaq's gain for 2026. The S&P 500 shed about $2.4 trillion in market value on the day and closed in a correction, 10% below its Oct. 6 record, for the first time since April 2025.

The Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) finished just shy of a bear market, or a 20% drop from its record closing high. Meanwhile, chip stocks had their worst week since the one after the 9/11 attacks.

The strange part is the timing. This was supposed to be a showcase week for AI. Nvidia's ( NVDA ) first report since Jensen Huang's exit showed revenue more than doubling, and Anthropic ( ANT ) pulled off the biggest IPO ever . Both stocks sank anyway.

Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its Oct. 6 top, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. Broadcom ( AVGO ), Micron ( MU ) and AMD ( AMD ) each fell about 12% to 14% Friday alone. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost about $1.5 trillion on the day, and the reasons keep piling up .

The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell about 17% this week and has lost a third of its value since Sept. 30. That puts chips on track for their worst two months since late 2008, a pace topped only in the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. Chips hit their financial-crisis low 18 years ago to the day, on Nov. 20, 2008.

The Nasdaq 100 and the tech sector are on the same track. The S&P 500 is headed for its worst November since 1973, and the Nasdaq for its worst since 2000. The S&P 500 has given up about $8 trillion since its record, nearly $6 trillion of it this week.

That's where the 2008 comparison breaks down. In October and November 2008, the typical S&P 500 stock lost about 28%. This time, the equal-weight S&P 500 ( RSP ) is about flat since Sept. 30.

Walmart ( WMT ) and Costco ( COST ) are rising Friday. A Goldman Sachs version of the S&P 500 that leaves out AI stocks is only about 5% below its record, Jim Bianco noted .

articles.title: 'Very interesting': Trump suggests recent gas price drops are linked to the election
articles.summary: President Trump on Tuesday escalated a suggestion he has been making in recent days on social media that the recent dip in energy prices is being driven by p...
articles.body:
President Trump on Friday escalated a suggestion he has been making on social media that the recent dip in energy prices is being driven by political forces now that the midterm election is in the rearview mirror.

"Crude oil prices have plummeted right since the end of the election: I wonder how that happened?" Trump said during a press conference to discuss this week's trip to Asia . "Too bad we didn't have that in front of the election, but that's the way it goes."

The president then made his insinuation more direct, comparing the price drop to the time Pfizer's ( PFE ) COVID vaccine was unveiled days after the 2020 election.

"I know the system," Trump said about the recent gas price decline. "Let's not call it corrupt, let's call it very interesting."

The remarks were an escalation of a claim Trump has been making on Truth Social over the last week , though there is no clear evidence that global energy markets have shifted in recent weeks based on US political factors .

The most recent figures from AAA show the national average gas price is now below $3.70 per gallon, the lowest since March, soon after the War in Iran began.

"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, in a recent newsletter. Seasonal factors and more oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz are more important, he wrote.

Gas prices have also historically declined in the fall after the summer driving season, due to a variety of factors.

At another point during Friday's press conference, Trump said crude oil prices had gone up less than he thought; he had expected them to top $300 a barrel after hostilities in Iran began.

Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Nvidia stock extends $2.7 trillion rout as SEC probe reportedly investigates its accounting
articles.summary: Nvidia's record sell-off deepened as Reuters reported that SEC investigators are examining its accounting.
articles.body:
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock fell nearly 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.

The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $485 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple ( AAPL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).

Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.

Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.

Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.

Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO.

The sell-off spread across chip stocks , which had their worst week since 2001 , and the broader market.

Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report.

"Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.

articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Sells $3.79 Billion, Making It Biggest Entertainment Launch Ever
articles.summary: The best-reviewed game ever is also the fastest-selling
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Take-Two Interactive Software Inc. said its new release Grand Theft Auto VI has generated $3.79 billion in revenue worldwide through the end of the day on Thursday's launch, making it the most successful entertainment property in history.

The company said it sold 32.5 million units in presales, also a record. A PC version of the game is expected to be released at a later date, as is an online component. The game costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for a package that includes a bonus vehicle, weapons, outfits and other in-game items.

Take-Two shares reversed losses earlier in the day and were up about 2.7% in New York trading.

Anticipation was significant going into Thursday's release. It's been 13 years since the last fully new addition to the Grand Theft Auto franchise, one of the most popular ever. The new game allows players to explore and rob their way through a fictional version of Miami called Vice City. Take-Two's subsidiary Rockstar Games, which now has more than 4,700 employees, spent more than eight years developing the game. The reviews have been the highest ever for a video game, with Bloomberg calling it "a masterpiece."

"This is a new platform for Rockstar to build more games and build on top, with really high fidelity," Wedbush Securities analyst Alicia Reese said in a Bloomberg TV interview on Friday before the sales were announced. "This should benefit Take-Two for years to come."

The release has turned into a popular culture moment. Take-Two paid for a marketing takeover of Miami, which celebrated the release even as it faced backlash from some residents. The NBA's Miami Heat played a game Wednesday in an arena bedecked with references to the game. Take-Two plans a concert Saturday in the city. Online influencers have been streaming marathon sessions of their gameplay on sites like Amazon.com Inc.'s Twitch and Alphabet Inc.'s YouTube.

Many fans of the game took Thursday off of work to play the game, which is also expected to eat into family time over the coming Thanksgiving weekend.

Grand Theft Auto V, the previous game in the franchise, generated sales of $800 million in its first 24 hours and $1 billion over three days after its 2013 debut.

articles.body:
Stocks have taken heavy losses this week, despite Anthropic going public after a record-setting initial public offering (IPO).

The Nasdaq composite , which hit an all-time high in early October, is now in the red since the start of the year. As of midafternoon Friday, the index had dipped by more than 4,700 points since closing at a record high of 27,599.886 on Oct. 6.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 were both in correction territory as of Friday afternoon.

Relative to the closing bell Aug. 5, the Dow was down by roughly 10.7 percent. The index Friday fell below 49,000 for the first time since late April.

The S&P 500 is also down by about 10.9 percent since it reached an all-time high Oct. 6, a banner day for the stock market. The S&P has not closed out a week under 7,000 since April 10.

“AI is melting down and the S&P 500 is in correction territory,” Callie Cox, the director of investment strategy at Plancorp Wealth Management, wrote in a Friday note.

Stocks have fallen throughout the week, with Anthropic going public Thursday failing to stop the bleeding.

The artificial intelligence giant raised $81.3 billion before it went live on the Nasdaq, after the company and certain stockholders sold 980 million shares of the company’s stock valued at $83 per share.

After underwriters exercised their option to purchase additional shares, the total amount Anthropic raised during its IPO reached $93.5 billion, the firm said in a Friday release . That surpassed Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised about $86 billion earlier this year, for the highest IPO on record .

President Trump on Friday credited Anthropic for its “very successful” opening, saying he has a “lot of respect” for co-founder Dario Amodei.

As of Friday afternoon, Anthropic’s stock was down roughly $10.30 from Thursday’s closing bell, after rising from a low of $83.05. Anthropic was trading at about $86.90 per share as of the afternoon.

Tech analyst Dan Ives chalked up the rough week for the markets, and specifically tech stocks , to a “perfect storm.”

That storm included Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories and “fears about an anti-AI/anti-datacenter DC,” Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia and Anthropic’s IPO “being a massive success but marginally reducing liquidity from other tech names,” Ives wrote Friday on social platform X.

Cox added, “Wall Street seems to be at the mercy of tech investors who think Jensen’s infidelity and Anthropic’s blockbuster market debut may be signs of a top.”

Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., also said “hawkish” rhetoric from Federal Reserve officials contributed to the rough week for stocks.

Amid persistent inflation , the Fed raised interest rates by a quarter point in September. Traders are pricing in a 90.1 percent chance of central bank officials doing so again in early December, after they held rates steady in late October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .

But Ives remained optimistic, writing Friday the $4 trillion AI build-out that he has predicted will reshape multiple industries is “still happening.”

articles.title: Senior Citizens League stimulus proposal: $1,400 checks for Social Security recipients
articles.summary: Here’s why a senior citizen advocacy group is proposing a $1,400 stimulus for retirees.
articles.body:

An advocacy group for American senior citizens is issuing a proposal for the incoming Congress: a one-time $1,400 stimulus to help seniors keep up with inflation.

The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) is an advocacy group representing older Americans. It is primarily focused on Social Security and Medicare benefits, as well as military and veteran benefits.

The stimulus proposal hasn't been introduced into any legislation, but the organization is turning to the incoming Congress for reform.

"The incoming class of Senators face an enormous responsibility," TSCL executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement. "Americans have chosen these elected representatives to protect seniors' dignity and rights, to protect benefits for today's retirees while reforming Social Security taxes to ensure the program continues to serve generations to come."

TSCL's proposed one-time $1,400 stimulus would go to all American retirees who receive Social Security benefits. The check, the group says, would "help make up for inadequate COLAs and rising inflation."

One reason seniors have been hit particularly hard by persistent inflation is rising medical costs. According to the most recent Consumer Price Index data, medical costs are still increasing. While prices increased by 0.4% overall month over month, medical care items increased by 0.5%, medical services increased by 0.3%, and hospital services increased by 0.8%.

At the same time, Medicare costs are also rising. Medicare Part B premiums will increase by $6.50 per month, or about 3.2% in 2027. The annual deductible for beneficiaries will increase by $9 in 2027.

To help offset inflation, the Social Security Administration already makes an annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for beneficiaries. The COLA for 2027 is 3.6% — the highest since 2023 and enough to add an average of $75 per month to the benefits seniors receive.

However, advocates say the COLA isn't enough to keep up , given factors like inflation and rising Medicare premiums. That's where the proposed stimulus can help, according to TSCL.

"This one-time, lump-sum, and tax-exempt payment would pay retirees back at least some of their Social Security benefits' lost value," Benton wrote in a statement .

The $1,400 senior stimulus is one part of a broader call to action TSCL is making to the incoming Congress. These are the other changes the group is advocating for:

Lift or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax threshold

Restore Medicare and Medicaid budget cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)

Add coverage for dental, vision, and hearing to Medicare benefits

articles.title: CrowdStrike Is in Talks to Buy Cybersecurity Firm Zscaler
articles.summary: CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is in talks to acquire Zscaler Inc., according to people familiar with the matter, in a deal that would be among the largest-ever i...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is in talks to acquire Zscaler Inc., according to people familiar with the matter, in a deal that would be among the largest-ever in the cybersecurity sector and create a company with a combined market value of about $265 billion.

The two companies are discussing a potential combination that could come together soon, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is confidential.

Deliberations are ongoing and there's no certainty they'll result in a transaction, the people said. Representatives for CrowdStrike and Zscaler didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Zscaler makes software that helps businesses protect against online threats. Its shares have dropped 13% this year, giving it a market value of $32 billion.

CrowdStrike, one of the cybersecurity industry's most valuable companies, has a market capitalization of around $233 billion. Through its core Falcon product, it specializes in endpoint security, or protecting individual devices like laptops and servers.

articles.title: ‘GTA VI’ sales blew past $3 billion in its first day, making it one of the biggest entertainment launches ever
articles.summary: A video game that fans had waited more than a decade for generated more revenue in its first day on the market than a Taylor Swift tour and a Marvel “Avengers” movie.
articles.body: A video game that fans had waited more than a decade for generated more revenue in its first day on the market than a Taylor Swift tour and a Marvel “Avengers” movie. “Grand Theft Auto VI” sales reached $3.79 billion after its first day of release, publisher Take Two Interactive and studio Rockstar Games announced on Friday, making it one of the biggest entertainment launches in history. The “Grand Theft Auto” series was already among the top-selling video game franchises. But a 13-year wait and a massive production budget heightened expectations and anticipation among fans. The game generated $2.36 billion in revenue before its November 19 release date, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Take Two said it sold 32.5 million pre-order copies, and the game has been available for preorder since June. “Avengers: End Game” grossed $2.9 billion at the box office, and Taylor Swift’s Eras tour generated roughly $2 billion in sales. The release has helped vault “GTA” from a video game to a “multigenerational franchise” on par with James Bond, Star Wars and Mickey Mouse, Omar Dessouky, a research analyst for Bank of America Global Research, wrote in a Friday research note. Beyond sales, the game also shattered live-streaming records on Twitch, YouTube and Kick, with fans collectively spending more than 132 million hours watching the game on its launch day, according to analytics platform Stream Charts. Set in “Vice City,” a fictionalized depiction of Miami, the game centers on two characters, Jason and Lucia, who find themselves in the center of a criminal conspiracy. “GTA” games are known for their crime-ridden missions and storylines and graphic content, but their realism is also a major part of what makes them resonate with players. “GTA 6” is filled with mundane activities — from bird watching to hitting the gym and hanging drywall — that can make players feel more connected to the game’s world and its characters. The game is expected to be a major driver of video game spending heading into the holiday season, with the only other major release in the fall timeframe being Nintendo’s “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” remake. More than 80% of those who preordered are splurging on the pricier $100 Ultimate Edition, which includes a range of extra cars and clothing and style customizations, compared to the $80 standard version, according to Sensor Tower. Bank of America’s Dessousky believes “GTA 6” could draw new audiences into gaming while pleasing longtime fans. “More mature storytelling should reengage lapsed gamers, including those who have not owned consoles in over a decade, while state of the art graphics and open world mayhem retain and attract younger audiences,” he wrote.
